title: How To Keep Your Class Improving
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a simple daily practice for keeping a class continually improving: maintaining a running 'like/don't like' list on a sheet of paper carried through the day, noting three specific things observed positively and three specific things that fell short of the standard. He stresses that the list must be honest, never inflating the 'like' column beyond genuinely excellent performance, because its core function is accurate feedback rather than encouragement for its own sake. The following day, the teacher shares both halves of the list directly with students, praising specific successes and naming specific areas expected to improve, giving the class a concrete target rather than vague encouragement. He argues many classes underperform simply because students don't know precisely what the teacher wants, and the list closes that gap through daily repetition. The piece frames this as a mechanism of continual striving that pushes a class toward ever-higher standards throughout the year.
points: A daily 'like/don't like' list, split into three genuine positive observations and three specific shortfalls, provides ongoing accurate feedback to a class.
The 'like' column must be reserved strictly for performance that truly reaches the standard of excellence, or the list loses its function as honest feedback.
Sharing both halves of the list directly with students the next day gives them a concrete, specific target rather than vague praise or criticism.
Many classes underperform simply because students don't know precisely what the teacher wants; the list closes that communication gap.
Using the list daily creates a mechanism of continual striving that pushes the class toward progressively higher standards over the school year.
quotes: One way to make this daily push for improvement easy is to maintain what I call a like/don’t like list.
Now, it’s important to mention that you must never put anything on your like list that doesn’t reach the level of excellence you’re striving for. First and foremost, the list is a method of feedback.

Yesterday, I liked how quickly you formed groups and got down to work. I want to see the same today. I also liked how you focused silently as I gave directions to the writing assignment. Today, I want to see the same attentiveness whenever I speak.

The truth is, many classes struggle because they don’t know what the teacher wants. The like/don’t like list is an easy way to ensure you’re giving pointed feedback while at the same time providing your students a target to shoot for.
It forces improvement day after day and allows you to push for greater and greater levels of excellence as the year goes on.
